name: Phosphatidic acid

card.summary: A membrane lipid sold as a pre-workout supplement because it signals to mTOR in cells; direct human evidence for added muscle is small and thin.
card.note: Cell-biology findings on mTOR are well established; evidence that oral supplements add muscle in people rests on very few small trials.

quick.overview:
Phosphatidic acid (PA) is a naturally occurring phospholipid found in every cell membrane. It is also sold as an over-the-counter supplement marketed to people who lift weights, on the premise that it activates the mTOR growth pathway.

The cell-biology link between PA and mTOR is well documented. Whether swallowing PA raises PA levels in muscle, and whether that produces extra muscle in people, has been tested in only a few small trials, and the ClinicalTrials.gov registrations for such studies are small.
quick.mechanism: In cell experiments, PA binds a domain of the mTOR protein and is needed for mitogen-driven activation of mTOR signaling, which regulates protein synthesis and cell growth [1][2]. Supplement proponents extrapolate from this to muscle growth after resistance training. Other work shows mTORC1 controls the location of lipin 1, an enzyme that processes PA [3].
quick.risks: PA is sold as a dietary supplement in the US, where supplements are regulated as foods and manufacturers are responsible for confirming safety [4]. Published safety data for supplemental PA in healthy lifters are limited. Because it is a general cell-signaling lipid, its role in other tissues has been studied mainly in laboratory research.

lead: Phosphatidic acid (PA) is the simplest glycerophospholipid: a glycerol backbone carrying two fatty acid chains and a phosphate group. It is a precursor for other membrane lipids and also acts as a signaling molecule inside cells.[5][6] Supplement makers sell it, usually extracted from soy or egg lecithin, to people who lift weights, who take it around training with the aim of adding muscle size and strength and so a fuller physique.[7]

The marketing rationale draws on a 2001 Science paper reporting that PA binds mTOR and is required for its mitogen-driven activation in cultured cells.[1] Resistance training itself switches on mTORC1 signaling and muscle protein synthesis, so the idea is that extra PA could amplify the post-workout growth signal.[7]

Two small randomized trials in resistance-trained men have tested PA products for eight weeks. One using PA alone found no difference from placebo in muscle thickness or strength; the other used a multi-ingredient product that also contained leucine, HMB and vitamin D3 and reported larger gains in lean mass and strength than placebo.[10][11] PA is sold as a dietary supplement in the US.[4]

paras: PA is made in cells by several routes: acylation of lysophosphatidic acid, cleavage of phosphatidylcholine by phospholipase D, and phosphorylation of diacylglycerol by diacylglycerol kinase. It is broken down to diacylglycerol or lysophosphatidic acid [5][6].

Its small headgroup shapes membrane curvature, and it recruits and regulates proteins, including mTOR, Raf1, protein kinase C epsilon and several ion channels [5][6]. Researchers still debate how much PA signals directly versus acting mainly as a precursor to diacylglycerol, and different fatty-acid species may have different activities [5].

The 2001 study reported that mitogen stimulation raised phospholipase D-dependent PA in cells, that this PA was required to activate mTOR effectors, and that PA interacted directly with the mTOR domain targeted by the drug rapamycin [1]. A 2011 Cell paper showed mTOR complex 1 in turn regulates the lipid-processing enzyme lipin 1, which converts PA to diacylglycerol, linking mTOR to lipid synthesis [2].

Resistance training activates mTORC1 signaling and muscle protein synthesis, which is the basis of the hypothesis that supplying PA could amplify that response [7]. Encyclopedia entries on the compound describe its cellular roles but do not address oral supplementation [5][6].

PA supplements are sold as powders or capsules, often branded with a trademarked soy-derived ingredient and marketed as pre-workout or post-workout products. Some products pair PA with leucine, HMB, creatine or caffeine in a multi-ingredient formula, which makes it hard to attribute a result to PA alone.[11]

Lecithin, which contains phosphatidylcholine and other phospholipids, is sometimes discussed as a cheaper dietary source; a T Nation forum user asked another whether lecithin granules taken for their PA content had produced any results.[12] Others on the same forum describe trying a PA product of their own, or ask whether anyone has experience with a micronized PA supplement.[13][14]

In an eight-week trial of 15 resistance-trained men (mean age about 23), participants took 750 mg of PA or placebo while training three days a week. Muscle thickness by ultrasound and one-rep-max squat, deadlift and bench press all rose in both groups, with no significant difference between PA and placebo; for example, squat 1RM rose 8.4% with PA and 8.1% with placebo.[10]

A double-blind trial of 18 strength-trained men tested a multi-ingredient product (PA plus L-leucine, HMB and vitamin D3) against placebo for eight weeks of three-day-per-week resistance training. The product group gained significantly more lean body mass and more leg press and bench press strength; fat mass, thigh muscle mass, vertical jump, agility and peak power did not differ between groups. The authors concluded that adding the product to a resistance program can improve lean mass and strength beyond exercise alone.[11]

Two registered trials exist: NCT03446924, a completed 16-participant study of PA's muscle-anabolic properties started in 2015, and NCT04277364, a 45-participant study of strength and hypertrophy begun in 2020 whose status is listed as unknown. Results are not posted in the registrations.[8][9] Registered trials of a PA-derived lipid in knee osteoarthritis address a different question and are not about muscle.[15]

In the US, dietary supplements are regulated as foods, with manufacturers responsible for confirming safety before sale.[4] The published trials above did not highlight adverse events in healthy trained men, but they were small and short, and long-term data on supplemental PA are limited.

Beyond sports nutrition, PA is studied as a cell-signaling lipid, including gating of ion channels such as PIEZO2, in nuclear envelope expansion and in cell division.[5][16] Investigators studying a PA-like compound in knee osteoarthritis have registered phase 1 and phase 1/2 trials.[15]

timeline.event: Early paper shows membrane phospholipids can activate a calcium-dependent protein kinase, part of the field linking lipids to signaling.[17]
Science paper identifies PA as a component of mitogenic mTOR signaling.[1]
Cell paper links mTORC1 to lipin 1, a PA phosphatase, and the SREBP lipid pathway.[2]
A small trial of PA's muscle-anabolic properties begins.[8]
Trial of a PA-containing multi-ingredient product reports lean mass and strength gains versus placebo.[11]
Trial of 750 mg PA in resistance-trained men reports no difference from placebo.[10]

lore.intro: PA appears in supplement marketing as an mTOR activator for lifters, and on T Nation it comes up in threads about pre-workout stacks and supplement experiments.[12][13][14]

claims.claim: Taking PA around training activates mTOR and adds extra muscle.
claims.believers: Proponents point to the cell studies showing PA binds and activates mTOR and reason that supplying more PA amplifies the post-workout growth signal.[1] One T Nation member planned a 30-day experiment with a 750 mg daily amount after a deload.[13]
claims.experts: The cell mechanism is published,[1][2] and in human trials a PA-alone product showed no difference from placebo while a multi-ingredient product showed larger lean mass and strength gains.[10][11]

claims.claim: Lecithin granules are a cheaper way to get PA.
claims.believers: Forum users have asked whether lecithin taken for its PA content produced results.[12]
claims.experts: No published human study has tested lecithin as a source of PA for muscle gain.

claims.claim: PA's cell biology means it can only help muscle.
claims.experts: Reviews describe PA as a broad signaling and membrane lipid with roles in many tissues, and its effects as a dietary supplement are mostly unstudied outside small trials.[5][6]
